title: The Pharaohs and the kings of Cush

intro.text: Scripture gives a personal name to five rulers of Egypt and Cush: Shishak, So, Tirhakah ("king of Ethiopia"), Pharaoh-nechoh and Pharaoh-hophra. Every other is "Pharaoh" or "the king of Egypt".

These nine pages run in the order of the story: the Pharaohs of Joseph, of the oppression and of the Exodus, Solomon's father-in-law, then the five named kings. The four unnamed Pharaohs have pages because the site's person data keeps a record for each; no page gives a king a name Scripture does not give, and every identification is shown as a view with its holders.

Other Pharaohs appear in one scene or one verse and are told on other pages or not at all: the Pharaoh who took Sarai and sent Abram away, the Pharaoh whose daughter Bithiah married Mered, the Pharaoh Rab-shakeh mocked as "this bruised reed" (see Tirhakah's page), and "Pharaoh king of Egypt" among the nations of Jeremiah's cup.
Zerah "the Ethiopian" came against Asa with a vast army of Ethiopians and Lubims and was routed at Mareshah; Scripture does not call him a king, so he has no page here.

Who Zerah was is a scholars' question: Petrie (1915) makes him Usarkon (Osorkon), Shishak's successor, invading in 903 BC; Cobern (1915) reports that most then identified him with Usarkon II, some with Usarkon I, and others with a ruler in Arabia.
"Pharaoh" is a title. Kyle (1915) explains it from the Egyptian for "great house", used first of the government and then of the king himself.

Scripture gives no Egyptian regnal years. The named kings carry the dates of a standard modern table (Hornung, Krauss and Warburton, 2006; facts only), with Breasted's 1906 dates and the 1915 encyclopaedia's beside them. The unnamed Pharaohs carry no dates, because their dates depend on who they were.

Where the Exodus falls is disputed: about 1448 BC if the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 are counted back (Mack, 1915), or in the 13th century BC under Merenptah (Driver, 1911). The views, with others, are on the Exodus Pharaoh's page.

rulers.name: Pharaoh of Joseph's day
rulers.title: King of Egypt (not named in Scripture)
rulers.tagline: The king who raised Joseph from the prison to rule Egypt.

identifications.text: Genesis calls him only "Pharaoh" and "Pharaoh king of Egypt". This page follows the person record that gathers Genesis 37–50 under one king; Scripture does not say whether the Pharaoh who let Joseph bury Jacob is the king who raised him.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign. "Pharaoh" raised Joseph at thirty and was still the title of the king who let Joseph bury Jacob, about twenty-six years later (Gen 41:46; 45:6; 47:28; 50:6).

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No name and no years. Any BC date depends on who he was; see the question below.

scriptureSays.text: He dreamed of seven fat and seven lean kine, and of full and thin ears, and none of the magicians or wise men of Egypt could interpret it.
Joseph told him: "God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do."
He asked his servants, "Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?"
He set Joseph over all Egypt: "only in the throne will I be greater than thou."
Jacob blessed Pharaoh when he came before him, and again when he went out.
Stephen: God "gave him favour and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and he made him governor over Egypt and all his house."
The psalm: "The king sent and loosed him; even the ruler of the people, and let him go free."

claim.text: The Midianites sold Joseph to Potiphar, "an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian".
Pharaoh was wroth with his chief butler and chief baker; on his birthday he restored the butler and hanged the baker, as Joseph had interpreted.
At the end of two full years Pharaoh dreamed, and no one in Egypt could interpret the dreams.
Joseph, brought out of the dungeon, told Pharaoh of seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and advised him to store a fifth of the land's produce.
Pharaoh gave Joseph his ring, fine linen, a gold chain and his second chariot, named him Zaphnath-paaneah and gave him Asenath, daughter of the priest of On.
In the seven plenteous years food was laid up in the cities, corn "as the sand of the sea".
When Egypt was famished the people cried to Pharaoh for bread, and he said, "Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do".
Hearing that Joseph's brothers had come, Pharaoh sent wagons for the family: "I will give you the good of the land of Egypt".
Pharaoh let Jacob's family dwell in Goshen, "in the best of the land", in "the land of Rameses".
Jacob, a hundred and thirty years old, stood before Pharaoh and blessed him.
In the famine Joseph bought the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, except the priests' land, and made it a law that Pharaoh should have the fifth part.
Pharaoh said, "Go up, and bury thy father", and his servants and the elders of Egypt went up with Joseph.

worship.text: Pharaoh spoke of Joseph as "a man in whom the Spirit of God is", because God had shown him the dreams' meaning.

building.text: Food was laid up "under the hand of Pharaoh" in the cities of Egypt.

alliances.text: He invited Jacob's household into Egypt and gave them Goshen; Joseph's brothers could be made "rulers over my cattle".

people.text: Joseph told his brothers to say they kept cattle, "for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians".
The Egyptians sold themselves and their land for bread: "we will be Pharaoh's servants".

claim.text: Jacob's household came from Canaan in the famine and settled in Goshen under Pharaoh's protection.
"All countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn; because that the famine was so sore in all lands."

views.label: A Hyksos king
views.holders: W. M. F. Petrie (1915); M. G. Kyle (1915); the Pulpit Commentary, naming Apophis; S. R. Driver (1911), on a late reckoning

argument.text: Petrie takes Joseph's title "Bow the knee" (Abrekh) for a Babylonian title of the Hyksos period; Kyle reads the note that Potiphar was "an Egyptian" as a sign of a foreign court; the Pulpit Commentary supposes Joseph to have been "the minister of Apophis, the last Hyksos king". Driver adds that a 13th-century Exodus and 430 years would bring Jacob to Egypt "c. 1660–40 B.C., while the foreign kings, called the Hyksos, were ruling", though he calls the 430 years "very uncertain".

views.label: A king of Manetho's list named by Ussher
views.holders: James Ussher (1650–54), as reported by John Gill

argument.text: Gill reports that Ussher, following Manetho's list, named the Pharaoh whose dreams Joseph interpreted Mephramuthosis, followed by Thmosis, Amenophis and Orus, in whose reign Joseph died.

notSaid: Scripture never gives this king's name.
Scripture does not say whether the Pharaoh who let Joseph bury Jacob (Gen 50:6) is the king who raised Joseph (Gen 41).
Scripture does not say when this king died; the next change it notes is "a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph", after Joseph and his generation had died (Exod 1:6, 8).
None of the records used for this page names Joseph or this king.

places.name: On (Heliopolis)
places.note: Home of Asenath's father, priest of On

rulers.name: Pharaoh of the oppression
rulers.title: King of Egypt (not named in Scripture)
rulers.tagline: The "new king" who set taskmasters over Israel and ordered the sons cast into the river.

identifications.text: This page follows the person record for the king of Exodus 1–2. Exodus says "the king of Egypt died" while Moses was in Midian, so the person data keeps the Pharaoh of the plagues as a separate record. Exodus does not say whether the "new king", the king who spoke to the midwives, and the Pharaoh who sought Moses' life when Moses was grown ("full forty years old", in Stephen's words) were one man.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length. The record runs from the start of the hard bondage, through Moses' birth and flight, to "the king of Egypt died" while Moses was in Midian (Exod 1:8–2:23).

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No name and no years. Stephen says Moses was forty when he fled and spent forty years in the wilderness before the bush (Acts 7:23, 29–30); any BC date depends on the date of the Exodus.

scriptureSays.text: "Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph."
He feared that Israel, "more and mightier than we", would join Egypt's enemies in war and leave the land.
He ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill the sons; when they did not, he charged all his people: "Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river".
When he heard that Moses had killed an Egyptian, "he sought to slay Moses".
Stephen: "The same dealt subtilly with our kindred, and evil entreated our fathers, so that they cast out their young children".
Moses' parents "were not afraid of the king's commandment".

claim.text: Taskmasters were set over Israel, and they built for Pharaoh the treasure cities Pithom and Raamses.
The Egyptians made Israel serve with rigour "in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field".
Shiphrah and Puah feared God and saved the boys alive, and told the king that the Hebrew women gave birth before they came.
Pharaoh charged all his people to cast every newborn son into the river.
Pharaoh's daughter found the child among the flags, had him nursed, and he became her son; she named him Moses.
Pharaoh sought to slay Moses, who fled to Midian.
"In process of time ... the king of Egypt died", and Israel's cry by reason of the bondage came up to God.

worship.text: "The midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them"; God dealt well with them.
Israel's cry came up to God, who "remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob".

building.text: Israel built Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh.

alliances.text: He feared Israel would "join also unto our enemies" in war.

people.text: "The more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew."
Their lives were made "bitter with hard bondage".

claim.text: Israel had multiplied in Egypt after Joseph's generation died.
Moses fled from Pharaoh to Midian and married the daughter of its priest.

A stela of Pharaoh Merneptah lists defeated peoples of Canaan: "Israel is desolated, his seed is not". Some read "his seed is not" as the killing of Israel's sons; Breasted (1906) answers that the phrase is conventional and used of other peoples too. The stela says nothing of a bondage in Egypt.

questions.question: Who was the "new king ... which knew not Joseph"?

views.label: Rameses Miamun

argument.text: Ussher, following Manetho's list of kings, writes that Rameses Miamun, who reigned sixty-six years, "is that new king, which knew not Joseph", and that the bondage went on for nineteen and a half years after his death, under his son Amenophis.

views.label: A native king who drove out the Hyksos

argument.text: The new king "can hardly be other than" the rise of the conquerors who took the Delta from the Hyksos at the start of the 18th dynasty (Petrie's date 1582 BC); the rigorous service came later, under Rameses II.

views.label: Thothmes III

argument.text: Taking the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 to run from Joshua's conquest rather than from the Exodus, Conder puts the Exodus about 1520 BC and makes Thothmes III, "a great enemy of the Asiatics", the Pharaoh of the oppression.

views.label: Rameses I or Seti I
views.holders: The Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott's commentary (Seti I)

argument.text: A new dynasty is meant; the founder of the 18th was a repairer of temples, not a builder of cities, so the new king was Rameses I or his son Seti I, and the city name Raamses points to that house.

views.label: Rameses II

argument.text: If the Israelites built Raamses and Pithom, "the Pharaoh of the oppression must have been Rameses II", since Pithom was founded by him (after Naville).

views.label: Cannot be decided

argument.text: A new dynasty is "very probable" but cannot be inferred with certainty from the word "new", and the want of trustworthy accounts of Egypt's kings "precludes the possibility of bringing this question to a decision".

questions.question: Does "a new king" mean a new royal house?

views.label: Yes, the crown had passed to another family

argument.text: Josephus writes that the Egyptians forgot Joseph's benefits, "particularly the crown being now come into another family".

views.label: Another king, of another mind or family

argument.text: "Another king; one of another disposition, or interest, or family".

questions.question: Who was the daughter of Pharaoh who raised Moses?

views.label: Thermuthis

argument.text: Josephus names her: "Thermuthis was the king's daughter".

views.label: Hatasu (Hatshepsut)

argument.text: On his early date, Moses was born under Thothmes III's sister Hatasu, regent for more than twenty years, who "might be the 'daughter of Pharaoh'".

notSaid: Scripture never gives this king's name, or his daughter's.
Scripture does not say how long he reigned or how long the hard bondage lasted under him.
Scripture gives two longer spans, not this reign's: Israel would be afflicted "four hundred years" (Gen 15:13), and the sojourning in Egypt was "four hundred and thirty years" (Exod 12:40).

rulers.name: Pharaoh of the Exodus
rulers.title: King of Egypt (not named in Scripture)
rulers.tagline: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go?"

identifications.text: This page follows the person record for the king Moses faced, from the burning bush to the sea (Exodus 3–15), with the later verses that look back to him. Exodus never names him.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length. Moses was eighty when he and Aaron spoke to him (Exod 7:7).

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No name and no years. 1 Kings 6:1 dates the start of Solomon's temple to "the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt"; how that is turned into a BC year, and which king it gives, are the views below.

scriptureSays.text: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the LORD, neither will I let Israel go."
Exodus says that Pharaoh hardened his heart, and that the LORD hardened it, as the LORD had told Moses beforehand.
After the hail he said, "I have sinned this time: the LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked".
At midnight of the last plague he called for Moses and Aaron: "Rise up, and get you forth from among my people ... and bless me also."
The LORD said to him, "for this cause have I raised thee up, for to shew in thee my power", words Paul quotes in Romans.
The psalm: the LORD "overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red sea".

claim.text: From the bush God sent Moses: "I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people".
Moses and Aaron asked leave for Israel to hold a feast in the wilderness; Pharaoh refused.
Pharaoh ordered that no straw be given yet the tale of bricks be kept: "Ye are idle, ye are idle".
Aaron's rod became a serpent and swallowed the magicians' rods; Pharaoh's heart was hardened.
The river was turned to blood; the magicians did the same, and Pharaoh went into his house.
Frogs covered Egypt; Pharaoh promised to let the people go, then hardened his heart when there was respite.
The magicians could not bring forth lice and said, "This is the finger of God".
Swarms of flies filled Pharaoh's house but not Goshen; he offered sacrifice "in the land", then said they should "not go very far away", and hardened his heart again.
The cattle of Egypt died but not Israel's; Pharaoh sent to see, and his heart was hardened.
Boils broke out on man and beast; the magicians could not stand before Moses.
Hail struck Egypt except Goshen; Pharaoh said "I have sinned this time", and when it ceased "he sinned yet more".
His servants urged him to let the men go; he offered to let the men only, and after the locusts said "I have sinned" again.
Three days' darkness, but Israel had light; Pharaoh would keep the flocks back and told Moses, "see my face no more".
At midnight the LORD smote all the firstborn "from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sat on his throne"; Pharaoh sent Israel out by night.
Told that the people had fled, he took six hundred chosen chariots and "all the chariots of Egypt" and overtook them by the sea.
The waters returned and "covered the chariots, and the horsemen, and all the host of Pharaoh ... there remained not so much as one of them".

worship.text: Moses asked to go "three days' journey into the wilderness" to sacrifice, since Israel's sacrifices would be "the abomination of the Egyptians".
The magicians copied the first signs, then said, "This is the finger of God".

building.text: Israel's officers were beaten when the tale of bricks was not met without straw.

alliances.text: Pharaoh's own servants said, "let the men go ... knowest thou not yet that Egypt is destroyed?"

people.text: Israel's officers told Moses and Aaron they had made Israel's savour "to be abhorred in the eyes of Pharaoh".
The Egyptians gave Israel jewels of silver and gold and raiment as they left.

claim.text: Sent to Pharaoh from the bush; again and again he carried the LORD's demand, "Let my people go", and warned of the plagues to come.

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness.

claim.text: The LORD made Moses "a god to Pharaoh", and Aaron his prophet to speak to Pharaoh.

quote.text: See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet.

claim.text: Israel went out "about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside children".
Jethro blessed the LORD "who hath delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of Pharaoh".

Pharaoh Merneptah's stela names "Israel" among peoples defeated in Canaan; Breasted (1906) called it the earliest mention of Israel then known. It names no Exodus, no Moses and no plagues; it bears on the date question below because it places Israel in Canaan in Merneptah's reign.
Josephus quotes the Egyptian priest Manetho's story of unclean people sent to the quarries under a king Amenophis and led by Osarsiph, whom Manetho made Moses; Josephus rejects it as fable.

questions.question: When was the Exodus, and under which king?

views.label: When the shepherds left under Tethmosis

argument.text: Josephus argues that Manetho's "shepherds", who left Avaris by agreement with king Thummosis and built Jerusalem, "were no other than our forefathers".

views.label: Amenophis, son of Rameses Miamun

argument.text: Ussher, following Manetho's list of kings, makes the king of the Exodus Amenophis, son and successor of Rameses Miamun: "he that was drowned in the red Sea".

views.label: In Egypt's 18th dynasty, counted from 1 Kings 6:1

argument.text: Mack counts the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 back from the founding of Solomon's temple (969 or 970 BC on his reckoning) and reaches "approximately 1448 BC". Conder takes the 480 years to run from Joshua's conquest, adds the forty years in the wilderness, puts the Exodus about 1520 BC, and makes its Pharaoh Amenophis II or Thothmes IV.

views.label: Late in the 18th dynasty, under Amenophis III
views.holders: J. Lieblein, as reported by C. R. Conder (1915)

argument.text: Conder reports that Lieblein placed the Exodus "late in the time of Amenophis III".

views.label: Under Merenptah, successor of Rameses II
views.holders: R. Lepsius (1840s), as reported by C. R. Conder; S. R. Driver (1911); W. M. F. Petrie (1915)

argument.text: Raamses (Exod 1:11) takes its name from Rameses II, who founded Pithom; Exodus 2:23 and 4:19 suggest the king of the Exodus was the oppressor's successor, Merenptah. Lepsius, as Conder reports, put the Exodus in 1314 BC, Merenptah's fifteenth year; Driver gives Merenptah 1234–1214 BC on Petrie's dates; Petrie puts the Exodus about 1220 BC.

notSaid: Scripture never gives this king's name or the length of his reign.

Exodus says the sea covered "all the host of Pharaoh that came into the sea after them" (14:28), and Psalm 136:15 that the LORD "overthrew Pharaoh and his host"; neither says in so many words that Pharaoh himself entered the sea or died.
Scripture gives no BC year for the Exodus.

places.name: Goshen
places.note: Spared the flies and the hail

places.name: Red Sea
places.note: Where his chariots and host were cast

rulers.name: Pharaoh, Solomon's father-in-law
rulers.title: King of Egypt (not named in Scripture)
rulers.tagline: He gave Solomon his daughter, and Gezer as her dowry.

identifications.text: The person record joins the Pharaoh whose daughter Solomon married (1 Kgs 3:1; 9:16) with the Pharaoh who sheltered Hadad the Edomite in David's day and made him his brother-in-law (1 Kgs 11:18–22). Scripture calls both only "Pharaoh king of Egypt" and does not say they were one man.

Tahpenes, called "the queen", is named only in 1 Kings 11:19–20. Ellicott's commentary calls it "a name unknown, either in history or in the Egyptian monuments"; the Pulpit Commentary, after R. S. Poole, says no name like it "has yet been found among those of the period".

reign.text: Scripture gives no length. The marriage falls early in Solomon's reign, before his house, the temple and the wall were finished (1 Kgs 3:1).

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No name and no years; any date depends on which king he was (see below).

scriptureSays.text: "And Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh's daughter, and brought her into the city of David."
"Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up, and taken Gezer, and burnt it with fire, and slain the Canaanites that dwelt in the city, and given it for a present unto his daughter, Solomon's wife."
The Pharaoh of Hadad's day gave the Edomite prince a house, food and land, and gave him "the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen".
When Hadad asked to go home, Pharaoh said, "But what hast thou lacked with me?"

claim.text: When Joab struck Edom in David's day, the child Hadad fled by Midian and Paran to Pharaoh, who gave him a house, victuals and land.
Pharaoh gave Hadad the sister of Queen Tahpenes; their son Genubath was weaned by Tahpenes and brought up "among the sons of Pharaoh".
Solomon "made affinity with Pharaoh" and brought his daughter into the city of David.
Pharaoh took Gezer, burnt it and slew its Canaanites, and gave it to his daughter; Solomon rebuilt it.
Hearing that David and Joab were dead, Hadad asked Pharaoh's leave to return to his own country.
Solomon built a house for Pharaoh's daughter, and she moved up into it out of the city of David.

worship.text: Chronicles: Solomon would not let his Egyptian wife live in the house of David, "because the places are holy, whereunto the ark of the LORD hath come".
Kings names "the daughter of Pharaoh" first among the "strange women" Solomon loved.

building.text: Solomon rebuilt Gezer, the city Pharaoh had given as a present.

alliances.text: A marriage alliance: "Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt".
Solomon's merchants brought horses and chariots out of Egypt, and passed them on to the kings of the Hittites and of Syria.

people.text: Hadad, sheltered in Pharaoh's court, became "an adversary unto Solomon".

claim.text: Solomon "reigned over all kingdoms from the river unto the land of the Philistines, and unto the border of Egypt".
Hadad, "of the king's seed in Edom", grew up in Pharaoh's court.
Tahpenes, called "the queen", weaned Hadad's son in Pharaoh's house.

first.text: Kings: "Pharaoh's daughter came up out of the city of David unto her house which Solomon had built for her".

second.text: Chronicles adds Solomon's reason: "My wife shall not dwell in the house of David ... because the places are holy".

views.label: Psusennes (Pasebkhanu) II, last of the 21st dynasty
views.holders: W. M. F. Petrie (1915); earlier Winer and Ewald, as reported by C. F. Keil (1872)

argument.text: Petrie gives Pasebkhanu II 987–952 BC and the marriage about 970; he adds that Hadad was first received by Siamen and married the queen's sister probably under Pasebkhanu. Keil reports Winer and Ewald for Psusennes, reasoning back from Shishak, who began the next dynasty.

views.label: Psinaches, the king before Psusennes

argument.text: Since Manetho gives Psusennes II only fourteen years, "it seems more probable that the princess whom Solomon married was the daughter of Psinaces who preceded Psusennes".

views.label: A late king of the 21st dynasty, not yet identifiable
views.holders: The Pulpit Commentary, after R. S. Poole

argument.text: Because Shishak began the 22nd dynasty, this Pharaoh was a late king of the 21st; but with Manetho's figures in conflict he "cannot yet be identified on Manetho's list".

notSaid: Scripture never gives this king's name, or the name of his daughter.
Scripture does not say whether the Pharaoh who sheltered Hadad in David's day is the Pharaoh whose daughter Solomon married.
Scripture does not say why Pharaoh attacked Gezer.

places.name: Gezer
places.note: Taken by Pharaoh, given as a dowry

rulers.name: Shishak
rulers.title: King of Egypt
rulers.tagline: He sheltered Jeroboam, then plundered Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year.

identifications.text: Shishak is identified with Shoshenq I, founder of Egypt's 22nd dynasty. Champollion, reading the Karnak relief in 1828, wrote that the identity he had proposed was confirmed there; Breasted (1906) and Nicol (1915) follow it.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length. He was already king while Solomon lived (1 Kgs 11:40) and came against Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year (1 Kgs 14:25).

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No regnal years. Scripture dates his invasion only by Rehoboam's fifth year (1 Kgs 14:25; 2 Chr 12:2).

dates.label: Hornung, Krauss and Warburton (2006), for Shoshenq I
Breasted (1906), for Shoshenq I
dates.note: Chronological table: "21 (+0?) years 945–924 B.C." He dates the campaign "probably about 926 B.C." (vol. IV §709).

dates.label: T. Nicol, ISBE (1915), for Shoshenq I

scriptureSays.text: Jeroboam "fled into Egypt, unto Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon".
"In the fifth year of king Rehoboam ... Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem" and took the treasures of the temple and the palace and Solomon's shields of gold.
Chronicles: he came "because they had transgressed against the LORD", with twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen and peoples without number: "the Lubims, the Sukkiims, and the Ethiopians".
Shemaiah: "Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak."
When Judah humbled itself, the LORD said his wrath would not be poured out "by the hand of Shishak. Nevertheless they shall be his servants".

claim.text: Jeroboam fled from Solomon to Shishak and stayed in Egypt until Solomon died.

events.label: The fenced cities of Judah taken

claim.text: He "took the fenced cities which pertained to Judah, and came to Jerusalem" (Chronicles).
Shemaiah told Rehoboam and the princes gathered at Jerusalem that God had left them in Shishak's hand; they humbled themselves.
He took the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the king's house, "he took all", with the gold shields Solomon had made.
Rehoboam made brass shields in place of the gold ones.

worship.text: Chronicles ties the invasion to Rehoboam's forsaking "the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him".
The king and princes humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous".

building.text: Rehoboam replaced Solomon's gold shields with brass.

alliances.text: Jeroboam, fleeing Solomon, went to Shishak and stayed in Egypt until Solomon's death.
Judah was to serve Shishak, "that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries".

people.text: His army brought "the Lubims, the Sukkiims, and the Ethiopians" (Chronicles).

claim.text: He told Rehoboam that Judah was left in Shishak's hand, and then that the LORD would grant "some deliverance".

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak.

claim.text: Jeroboam came back from Egypt at Solomon's death and was made king over Israel.
Rehoboam's Jerusalem was plundered in his fifth year.

On the outside south wall of Amun's temple at Karnak, Shoshenq I is shown smiting Asiatics while Amun and the goddess of Thebes lead 156 captives, each a ring holding a town's name. About 75 names survive, in two groups Breasted took as towns of Israel and of Judah (among them Taanach, Shunem, Beth-shean, Mahanaim, Gibeon, Beth-horon, Aijalon, Megiddo and Arad).

outside.name: What the Karnak list does not say

claim.text: No king of Judah or Israel is named, and Jerusalem is not among the names that can be read: "We look in vain for Jerusalem", Breasted wrote, supposing it lost in a gap. Champollion had read one ring as "the kingdom of Judah"; Breasted rejects that reading.
Dated in year 21, it records the cutting of stone for a great pylon and court at Karnak. Breasted held that the gate built then (the "Bubastite gate") received the campaign relief.

Josephus retells Kings and Chronicles, giving Shishak 400,000 footmen besides the chariots and horsemen, saying Herodotus wrongly credited his deeds to Sesostris, and that Rehoboam received him into the city without fighting.

first.text: Kings tells the invasion in four verses: Shishak came up and took the treasures and the gold shields.

second.text: Chronicles adds the army and its peoples, the taking of Judah's fenced cities, Shemaiah's message, the humbling and the partial deliverance.

first.text: Kings gives no reason for the invasion.

second.text: Chronicles: "because they had transgressed against the LORD".

views.label: Probably about 926 BC

argument.text: Breasted places the campaign in Rehoboam's fifth year, "probably about 926 B.C.", in the latter half of Shoshenq's reign, before the year-21 building that carried its relief.

views.label: About 926/925 BC
views.holders: Rehoboam's fifth year on McFall's revision of Thiele (1991)

argument.text: McFall's table starts Rehoboam in 931/930 BC, so Rehoboam's fifth year, when Scripture puts the invasion, falls about 926/925 BC.

views.label: Yes, the city was captured

argument.text: Shishak plundered the treasures of the temple and the palace, so he must have captured the city.

views.label: Spared destruction, but not surrender

argument.text: Jerusalem surrendered, but was preserved from destruction when the people repented at Shemaiah's call.

views.label: He was bought off

argument.text: Shishak was bought off with a heavy present, as Sennacherib later was by Hezekiah.

notSaid: Scripture does not say why Shishak sheltered Jeroboam.
Scripture does not say that Shishak fought for Jerusalem; both books say he "came up against Jerusalem" and took its treasures.
Scripture names none of the fenced cities he took.
None of the Egyptian records used for this page names Rehoboam or Jeroboam.

places.name: Thebes (Karnak)
places.note: Where the relief of the campaign is carved

places.name: Arad
places.note: On Shoshenq I's Karnak list (Breasted): the southernmost town he names

rulers.name: So
rulers.title: King of Egypt
rulers.tagline: Named once: Hoshea's appeal to him cost Israel its king.

identifications.text: Scripture names So once, as "So king of Egypt" (2 Kgs 17:4). Who he was is disputed. The views below are those of writers up to 1915 whose words could be read for this page. Other identifications have been proposed since, among them Osorkon IV, Tefnakht, and reading "So" as the city of Sais rather than a king; the modern works that argue them could not be opened and checked, so they are not set out here.

reign.text: Scripture gives no years; it names him once, in Hoshea's reign over Israel (2 Kgs 17:4).

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No regnal years. Who he was is disputed (see below), so no reign dates are given.

scriptureSays.text: "And the king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea: for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and brought no present to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year."
Scripture says nothing of any answer from So. The king of Assyria shut Hoshea up in prison, besieged Samaria three years and took it.

claim.text: Hoshea, Assyria's tributary, sent messengers to So and stopped his yearly present to Assyria.
The king of Assyria "shut him up, and bound him in prison".
Assyria besieged Samaria three years and in Hoshea's ninth year took it and carried Israel away.

alliances.text: Israel's king turned from Assyria to Egypt: "he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt".

people.text: Israel was carried away into Assyria, to Halah, Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes.

claim.text: Hosea, whose book is dated to the days of Jeroboam son of Joash and of Judah's kings down to Hezekiah, speaks of Ephraim calling to Egypt and Assyria by turns. He does not name So, and does not date these words to Hoshea's embassy.

quote.text: Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria.

claim.text: Hoshea, the last king of Israel, reigned nine years in Samaria.
"Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria; and Hoshea became his servant, and gave him presents."

outside.name: Sargon's annals: the battle at Raphia

claim.text: Sargon writes that Hanno of Gaza and Sib'e (Sib'u), "turtan of Egypt" (a commander), came out against him at Rapihu; Sib'e fled and Hanno was taken. In the broken annals passage Luckenbill has Sib'u order "his turtan" to Hanno's aid, while Rogers reads "Sib'u, his Tartan" called to Hanno's side; in both, Sib'u fled alone "like a shepherd". These records name no Hoshea and no king "So".
Sargon lists tribute from "Pir'u (Pharaoh), king of Egypt" with Samsi, queen of Arabia, and It'amra the Sabean. Luckenbill renders Pir'u as "Pharaoh": a title, with no personal name.

views.label: Shabaka (Sabaco), first king of the Ethiopian dynasty
views.holders: James Ussher (1658); Ellicott's commentary; the Pulpit Commentary; T. Nicol (1915)

argument.text: Ussher, citing Jerome's spelling of the name, took So to be "Sabacon the Ethiopian". Ellicott's commentary reads the Hebrew name as Seveh, the Egyptian Shabaka, "whom Sargon defeated at Raphia in 720 B.C."; the Pulpit Commentary says the Assyrians knew him as Sibakhi. Nicol, giving Shabaka 715–707 BC on Petrie's dates, supposes he could be called king while still regent.

views.label: Shabaka, as viceroy for his father

argument.text: Petrie writes that Shabaka was appointed viceroy of Egypt by his father Piankhy, and is the Assyrians' "Sibe, commander-in-chief of Muzri" and the Hebrews' "Sua or So".

views.label: Shabaka or his successor Sevechus; cannot yet be decided
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872), reporting Vitringa, Gesenius and Ewald for Sevechus

argument.text: So is "one of the two Shebeks" of the Ethiopian dynasty; whether Sabako or his son Sevechus (held by Vitringa, Gesenius, Ewald) "cannot possibly be decided in the present state of Egyptological research".

views.label: Perhaps the Egyptian general Sib'e of Sargon's records

argument.text: Lumby thinks Shebek or Shebetek most probable, but notes the Egyptian general "Sibakhi or Sibahe" of the Assyrian records, who helped the king of Gaza, and says "This may be the person here spoken of."

notSaid: No other verse names So.
Scripture does not say whether So answered Hoshea or sent any help.
Scripture does not say where So reigned or for how long.

places.name: Gaza
places.note: Hanno of Gaza fought beside Sib'e of Egypt (Sargon's annals)

rulers.name: Tirhakah
rulers.title: King of Ethiopia (Cush)
rulers.tagline: The news of his march made Sennacherib write to Hezekiah.

capital.name: Memphis
capital.note: Not named in Scripture; Esarhaddon calls Memphis "his royal city" (Luckenbill II §580).

identifications.text: Tirhakah is identified with Taharqa of the 25th (Kushite) dynasty, the "Tarkû, king of Egypt and Ethiopia" of Ashurbanipal's annals.

reign.text: Scripture gives no years. It names him twice, in one report, as "king of Ethiopia" (2 Kgs 19:9; Isa 37:9).

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No regnal years. Sennacherib's campaign against Judah, when Scripture names him, is fixed at 701 BC by the Assyrian annals.

dates.label: Hornung, Krauss and Warburton (2006), for Taharqa
Breasted (1906), for Taharka
dates.note: Chronological table: 688–663 B.C.

dates.label: T. G. Pinches, ISBE (1915)
dates.note: He died "after a reign of at least 26 years, in 667 BC", so came to the throne "about 693 BC".

scriptureSays.text: "And when he heard say of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, Behold, he is come out to fight against thee: he sent messengers again unto Hezekiah."
Isaiah's book gives the same report in nearly the same words.

Before this, Rab-shakeh had mocked Judah's trust in Egypt: "thou trustest upon the staff of this bruised reed, even upon Egypt ... so is Pharaoh king of Egypt unto all that trust on him". He names no Pharaoh.

claim.text: Rab-shakeh found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah, having left Lachish.
Word came that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia had come out to fight against the Assyrian king.
Hearing it, Sennacherib sent messengers to Hezekiah again: "Let not thy God in whom thou trustest deceive thee".
That night the angel of the LORD smote the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib returned to Nineveh. Scripture does not connect this with Tirhakah.

worship.text: Hezekiah spread Sennacherib's letter before the LORD and prayed.

alliances.text: Rab-shakeh accused Hezekiah of putting his "trust on Egypt for chariots and for horsemen".

claim.text: Isaiah's book repeats the report of Tirhakah. Elsewhere Isaiah warns those who go down to Egypt for help, and walked "naked and barefoot" as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia in the year Sargon's Tartan took Ashdod. These warnings are not dated to Tirhakah's march.

quote.text: Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many

claim.text: Hezekiah, in Jerusalem, received Sennacherib's second message.
Sennacherib went home to Nineveh, where his sons killed him, "and Esar-haddon his son reigned in his stead".

outside.name: Sennacherib's annals: the battle near Eltekeh

claim.text: Sennacherib writes that Ekron's leaders "called upon the Egyptian kings, the bowmen, chariots and horses of the king of Meluhha (Ethiopia)", and that he fought them near Eltekeh and won. He names neither Tirhakah nor any Egyptian king.

Breasted reads this broken stela as telling how Taharqa came north from Nubia "as a youth of twenty years with some king", and how his mother later came to him after his coronation. Breasted puts his accession "some thirteen years" after 701.

Esarhaddon claims to have struck Tarkû five times with javelins, taken "Memphis, his royal city" in half a day, and carried off his queen and his heir Ushanahuru. The relief shows a kneeling figure in shackles that Luckenbill takes for Tirhakah.

Ashurbanipal writes that Tarkû retook Memphis, was beaten at Kar-baniti and fled to Thebes; later "the night of death overtook him", and Tandamane took his throne ("son of Shabaku" in one text, "son of his sister" in another).

questions.question: Was Tirhakah already king when Sennacherib invaded in 701 BC?

views.label: A commander under Shabaka, called king by a later writer

argument.text: Taharqa came north at twenty with Shabaka and became king about thirteen years after 701; Shabaka must have sent him in command, and "the Hebrew writer, reporting the matter at a later date ... supposes him to have been already king".

views.label: Acting for the reigning Pharaoh before his own reign
views.holders: W. M. F. Petrie, as reported by T. G. Pinches (1915); Ellicott's commentary; the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Petrie supposed he acted at first for his kinsman Shabataka; Ellicott suggests he commanded in his father's name; the Pulpit Commentary has him ruling from Napata and over Egypt from about 700 with Shabatok as "a sort of puppet-king", succeeding about 693.

views.label: Two campaigns of Sennacherib have been run together
views.holders: A "general opinion" reported by T. G. Pinches (1915)

argument.text: Pinches reports "a general opinion" that the Assyrian historians, like those of Kings and Isaiah, "have mingled two campaigns made by Sennacherib, one of them being after the accession of Tirhakah".

notSaid: Scripture does not say that Tirhakah's army met the Assyrians, or what became of it.
Scripture does not say that Hezekiah asked Tirhakah for help.
Scripture calls him "king of Ethiopia", never "Pharaoh"; the Pharaoh Rab-shakeh mocked as "this bruised reed" is not named.

places.name: Eltekeh
places.note: Where Sennacherib fought the Egyptians and Ethiopians (his annals)

places.name: Memphis
places.note: Taken by Esarhaddon; retaken and lost again (Assyrian annals)

places.name: Thebes
places.note: Where he fled from Ashurbanipal (Assyrian annals)

rulers.name: Pharaoh Necho
rulers.title: King of Egypt
rulers.tagline: He killed Josiah at Megiddo, made and unmade Judah's kings, and lost at Carchemish.

identifications.text: Pharaoh-necho is identified with Necho II of Egypt's 26th dynasty, the Necos son of Psammetichos of Herodotus.
The person record also places under him "Pharaoh king of Egypt" in Jeremiah's oracle on Carchemish (Jer 46:17, 25), verses that do not name him.

reign.text: Scripture gives no years for him. Herodotus gives him sixteen years.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No regnal years. Scripture dates his deeds by Judah's kings: Josiah's death, Jehoahaz's three months, and Carchemish in Jehoiakim's fourth year (Jer 46:2).

dates.label: Hornung, Krauss and Warburton (2006), for Necho II
Breasted (1906)
dates.note: Chronological table: 609–593 B.C.

dates.label: T. Nicol, ISBE (1915)
dates.note: "610–594 BC"; Nicol dates Megiddo 608 and Carchemish 604.

scriptureSays.text: "In his days Pharaoh-nechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates: and king Josiah went against him; and he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him."

Chronicles gives his message to Josiah: "What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? I come not against thee this day, but against the house wherewith I have war: for God commanded me to make haste".
Chronicles says Josiah "hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God".
He bound Jehoahaz at Riblah, fined the land a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold, made Eliakim king and "turned his name to Jehoiakim".
Jeremiah: "the army of Pharaoh-necho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim".
"And the king of Egypt came not again any more out of his land: for the king of Babylon had taken from the river of Egypt unto the river Euphrates all that pertained to the king of Egypt."

claim.text: He went up "against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates" (Kings), "to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates" (Chronicles).
Josiah went out against him and was killed at Megiddo; Chronicles says archers wounded him and he died at Jerusalem.
After three months' reign Jehoahaz was put in bands at Riblah "that he might not reign in Jerusalem".
The land was fined a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold, which Jehoiakim raised by taxing the people.
He made Eliakim son of Josiah king and changed his name to Jehoiakim.
Jehoahaz was taken to Egypt "and died there"; Jeremiah said Shallum son of Josiah would not return.
Nebuchadrezzar smote Necho's army at Carchemish by the Euphrates in Jehoiakim's fourth year.
The king of Egypt came out of his land no more; Babylon held everything from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.

worship.text: Necho claimed a command from God; Chronicles calls his words "from the mouth of God".

alliances.text: Judah became Egypt's tributary under a king Necho chose: "Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh".

people.text: Jehoiakim "taxed the land ... of every one according to his taxation, to give it unto Pharaoh-nechoh".
"All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah."

claim.text: Jeremiah lamented Josiah, foretold that Jehoahaz would die in exile, and gave the oracle on Necho's army at Carchemish and on Pharaoh, "but a noise".

quote.text: They did cry there, Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise; he hath passed the time appointed.

claim.text: He killed one king of Judah, deposed the next, and set up a third.
Kings says he went up "against the king of Assyria", whom it does not name.
Nebuchadrezzar smote his army at Carchemish in "the fourth year of Jehoiakim", which Jeremiah calls "the first year of Nebuchadrezzar".

Herodotus makes Necos son of Psammetichos: he began a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, built triremes, "engaged battle at Magdolos with the Syrians, and conquered them; and after this he took Cadytis, which is a great city of Syria", and reigned sixteen years.

outside.name: Herodotus on the voyage round Libya

claim.text: Herodotus says Necos sent Phoenicians who sailed round Libya (Africa) and came home in the third year, reporting that they had the sun on their right hand, "a thing which I cannot believe".

outside.name: Babylonian chronicle of the fall of Nineveh

claim.text: A chronicle (British Museum 21901, published by Gadd in 1923) records that Assur-uballit, king of Assyria, and "the great army of Egypt" crossed the river and attacked Harran, without taking it. It does not name Necho, Josiah or Megiddo.

The chronicle (BM 21946) records that in Nabopolassar's 21st year the crown prince Nebuchadnezzar crossed the Euphrates against the Egyptian army at Carchemish, defeated it, and overtook its remnant in the district of Hamath; that year Nabopolassar died and Nebuchadnezzar took the throne. It does not name Egypt's king.

outside.name: Babylonian Chronicle 5: the clash of 601 BC

claim.text: In Nebuchadnezzar's fourth year the chronicle has him march toward Egypt; the king of Egypt met him in open battle, both sides suffered heavy losses, and Nebuchadnezzar went home and spent the next year refitting his chariots and horses.

outside.name: A Serapeum stela of his sixteenth year

claim.text: A stela for an Apis bull that died "in the sixteenth year of Necho" lets Breasted compute the reign of Necho's father Psamtik I.

first.text: Kings: "against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates".

second.text: Chronicles: "to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates", with his message to Josiah that he came "against the house wherewith I have war".

first.text: Kings: Necho "slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him"; he was carried dead to Jerusalem.

second.text: Chronicles: Josiah disguised himself, was shot by archers in the valley of Megiddo, and died after being brought to Jerusalem.

first.text: Kings: Pharaoh-nechoh "put him in bands at Riblah in the land of Hamath, that he might not reign in Jerusalem".

second.text: Chronicles: "the king of Egypt put him down at Jerusalem".

questions.question: Who was the "king of Assyria" Necho went up against?

views.label: The king of Babylon, ruling Assyria's empire

argument.text: "King of Assyria" means the Babylonian king, probably Nabopolassar.

views.label: The last king of Assyria

argument.text: Necho's enemy was the last king of Nineveh, then at war with Nabopolassar.

views.label: Cannot be determined

argument.text: It depends on the year Nineveh fell, which Keil could not fix.

questions.question: Is Herodotus's battle at "Magdolos" Josiah's Megiddo, and is "Cadytis" Gaza?

views.label: Magdolos is Megiddo
views.holders: John Hudson, as reported by William Whiston (1737)

argument.text: Whiston's note on Josiah's death: the battle "is justly esteemed the very same that Herodotus ... mentions", at "Magdolum, [Megiddo,]", "as Dr. Hudson here observes".

views.label: Cadytis is Gaza
views.holders: Hitzig, as reported in Ellicott's commentary; A. W. Streane (1881)

argument.text: Hitzig identified Cadytis with Gaza, taken on Necho's return from Carchemish; Streane takes it as Gaza, taken after Megiddo.

views.label: Cadytis is not shown to be Gaza

argument.text: Keil writes that "neither Hitzig nor Stark have proved the identity of Kadytis with Gaza", so nothing can be safely drawn from Herodotus on when Gaza was taken.

notSaid: Scripture does not say why Josiah went out against Necho.
Scripture does not say whether Necho reached the Euphrates in the year Josiah died, or what he did there.
Scripture does not name Necho in the account of Carchemish outside Jeremiah 46:2.

places.name: Haran
places.note: Harran, attacked by Assyria and Egypt in 609 BC (Babylonian chronicle)

rulers.name: Hophra
rulers.title: King of Egypt
rulers.tagline: Zedekiah's ally, given "into the hand of his enemies".

identifications.text: Pharaoh-hophra is identified with Apries, as Herodotus calls him, the Wahibre of the monuments.

Scripture names Hophra only at Jeremiah 44:30. The person record gathers to him the unnamed "Pharaoh" of Jeremiah 37, 43 and 47 and of Ezekiel 17 and 29–32. Commentators identify Ezekiel's Pharaoh with Hophra (Poole; Gill), and the Pharaoh whose army came out during the siege with him too (Rogers 1912; Nicol 1915; Ellicott's commentary).

reign.text: Scripture gives no years for him. Herodotus gives Apries twenty-five years.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: No regnal years. Scripture's nearest dates are Ezekiel's, counted from Jehoiachin's captivity: oracles against Pharaoh in the tenth, eleventh and twelfth years (Ezek 29:1; 30:20; 31:1; 32:1).

dates.label: Hornung, Krauss and Warburton (2006), for Apries
Breasted (1906)
dates.note: Chronological table: 588–569 B.C.

dates.label: T. Nicol, ISBE (1915)
dates.note: "He reigned alone from 589 BC to 570 BC", then jointly with Amasis for some years.

scriptureSays.text: "Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will give Pharaoh-hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, and into the hand of them that seek his life; as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon."
"Pharaoh's army, which is come forth to help you, shall return to Egypt into their own land."

Ezekiel: Zedekiah rebelled by "sending his ambassadors into Egypt, that they might give him horses and much people", but "Neither shall Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company make for him in the war".
Ezekiel to "Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers, which hath said, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself".
"I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt" (Ezekiel, in the eleventh year).

claim.text: Zedekiah broke his oath to Babylon by sending ambassadors to Egypt for horses and men.
Pharaoh's army came forth out of Egypt, and the Chaldeans besieging Jerusalem departed "for fear of Pharaoh's army".

events.label: Jeremiah: the army will go home

claim.text: Jeremiah told Zedekiah's messengers that Pharaoh's army would return to Egypt and the Chaldeans would come back and burn the city.
Ezekiel prophesied against "Pharaoh king of Egypt" in the tenth, eleventh and twelfth years of the captivity.
After Gedaliah's murder the remnant, fearing the Chaldeans, went to Egypt against Jeremiah's word and came to Tahpanhes.

events.label: Stones at Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes

claim.text: Jeremiah hid great stones "at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes": Nebuchadrezzar would set his throne on them.
To the Jews living in Egypt, Jeremiah gave a sign: Pharaoh-hophra would be given into his enemies' hand.

worship.text: The Jews in Egypt told Jeremiah they would go on burning incense "unto the queen of heaven"; the sign of Hophra was the LORD's answer.

alliances.text: Zedekiah looked to Egypt for "horses and much people".
Ezekiel calls Egypt "a staff of reed to the house of Israel".

people.text: Jews settled "at Migdol, and at Tahpanhes, and at Noph, and in the country of Pathros".

claim.text: He foretold that Pharaoh's army would go home, warned the remnant not to go to Egypt, and named Hophra in the sign of Jeremiah 44:30.

quote.text: Behold, I will give Pharaoh-hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, and into the hand of them that seek his life

claim.text: Among the captives in the land of the Chaldeans, he denounced Zedekiah's appeal to Egypt and spoke dated oracles against "Pharaoh king of Egypt", whom he does not name.

quote.text: Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers

claim.text: Zedekiah's revolt ended with Jerusalem's fall; after Gedaliah's murder Johanan led the remnant into Egypt.
Jeremiah foretold that Nebuchadrezzar would smite Egypt and spread his pavilion at Tahpanhes.

Herodotus makes Apries son of Psammis: he reigned twenty-five years, marched against Sidon and fought the king of Tyre at sea. After a disastrous expedition against Cyrene the Egyptians revolted and made Amasis king.

Beaten by Amasis at Momemphis, Apries was kept in the palace at Sais; at last Amasis gave him up to the Egyptians, "and they strangled him". Herodotus adds that Apries "is said to have supposed that not even a god would be able to cause him to cease from his rule".

Breasted reads this badly worn stela as telling that Apries came with Greeks and ships against Amasis, was defeated, and was later slain; Amasis buried him as a king. Breasted finds it hard to harmonise with Herodotus on how Apries died.

Josephus writes that in Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year he fell upon Egypt, "slew the king that then reigned, and set up another", naming neither. Whiston's note applies it to Hophra and observes that Herodotus has him slain by the Egyptians.

views.label: Strangled by the Egyptians

argument.text: Taken alive by Amasis and kept at Sais, he was handed over to the Egyptians, who strangled him and buried him with his fathers.

views.label: Killed in a later war with Amasis
views.holders: Amasis's stela, as read by J. H. Breasted (1906)

argument.text: Three years into Amasis's reign Apries returned with Greek troops and ships, was defeated, and was afterwards slain; Amasis gave him a king's burial.

views.label: Slain by Nebuchadnezzar

argument.text: Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar slew "the king that then reigned" in Egypt; he does not name him.

views.label: Necho, on his return from Carchemish
views.holders: Hitzig, as reported in Ellicott's commentary; John Gill (1748–63)

argument.text: Taking Herodotus's Cadytis for Gaza, Hitzig dates the attack to Necho's return from Carchemish; Gill thinks it "more likely" Necho, going to or returning from Carchemish.

views.label: Necho, after Megiddo, in a scribe's note

argument.text: The words "before that Pharaoh smote Gaza" are missing from the Greek and are probably "a gloss added by a scribe" who thought of Necho's capture of Kadytis after Megiddo.

views.label: Hophra
views.holders: Calvin, as reported by Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); C. F. Keil (1874), after Rashi and Perizonius

argument.text: Necho could not have taken Gaza after Carchemish, since "the king of Egypt came not again any more out of his land"; Hophra, who sought to win back Egypt's power in Asia, may have taken it, perhaps on returning from his attempt to relieve Jerusalem.

notSaid: Scripture does not tell how Jeremiah 44:30 was fulfilled.
Scripture does not name the Pharaoh whose army came out during the siege (Jer 37:5), or say whether it fought the Chaldeans.
Ezekiel never names the Pharaoh of his oracles.
Scripture foretells, but does not narrate, Nebuchadrezzar's attack on Egypt (Jer 43:10–13; Ezek 29:19).
